Zarephath
ZAIR-uh-fath
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Tsarephath (H6886), "smelting place, refinery" (from tsaraph, "to smelt, refine"). A Phoenician town on the Mediterranean coast between Tyre and Sidon; Greek Sarepta (Luke 4:26).

📖 Biblical Definition

Zarephath was a Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon — outside the land of Israel, in Gentile territory — where the prophet Elijah was sent during the great drought to be sustained by a poor widow, and where the LORD worked the miracle of the never-failing meal and oil and raised the widow's son from death. When the brook Cherith dried up, "the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee" (1 Kings 17:8-9). Elijah found the widow gathering sticks to prepare a last meal for herself and her son before they died of the famine; he asked her first to make him a small cake, with the promise, "The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth" (1 Kings 17:14). She believed and obeyed, and the meal and oil did not fail through the whole drought — God sustaining the prophet, the widow, and her household by a daily miracle of provision that rewarded her faith. Later, when the widow's son fell sick and died, Elijah stretched himself upon the child and cried to the LORD, who restored the boy to life — the first resurrection recorded in Scripture (1 Kings 17:17-24). The significance of Zarephath is heightened by the Lord Jesus's own use of it. In the synagogue at Nazareth, rebuking His own townspeople's unbelief, He pointed to Zarephath: "many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias... But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow" (Luke 4:25-26). The point was sharp and offensive to the Nazarenes: God in His sovereign grace passed by the widows of Israel and sent His prophet to a Gentile widow of Zarephath — a foreshadowing of the gospel going to the Gentiles, and a rebuke to those who presumed on covenant privilege while rejecting the LORD. Zarephath ("refinery") was the place where a Gentile widow's faith was refined and rewarded, and where sovereign grace reached beyond the borders of Israel.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Phoenician (Gentile) town between Tyre and Sidon where Elijah was sustained by a widow during the drought, by the miracle of the never-failing meal and oil, and where he raised her son (the first resurrection, 1 Kings 17); cited by the Lord Jesus as sovereign grace reaching a Gentile (Luke 4:25-26).

ZAREPHATH, proper noun. Hebrew Tsarephath (H6886), "smelting place, refinery"; Greek Sarepta; a Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon.

Outside Israel, in Gentile territory; where Elijah was sent during the drought to a widow commanded to sustain him (1 Kings 17:8-9).

The miracle of the never-failing barrel of meal and cruse of oil, rewarding the widow's faith (1 Kings 17:14-16).

Where Elijah raised the widow's dead son — the first resurrection recorded in Scripture (1 Kings 17:17-24).

Cited by the Lord Jesus as sovereign grace reaching a Gentile widow while passing by the widows of Israel (Luke 4:25-26).

📖 Key Scripture

1 Kings 17:9 — "Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee."

1 Kings 17:14 — "For thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth."

1 Kings 17:22-23 — "And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived... and Elijah... delivered him unto his mother: and Elijah said, See, thy son liveth."

Luke 4:25-26 — "But I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias... But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Zarephath is corrupted when the widow's faith is read as mere folklore, when the never-failing meal is spiritualized away from God's real provision, or when the Lord Jesus's point about sovereign grace to the Gentiles is blunted to spare covenant presumption.

expand to see more

Sovereign-grace point blunted. The Lord Jesus's use of Zarephath in the Nazareth synagogue was deliberately offensive to His hearers: He reminded them that in the days of Elijah, when many Israelite widows were in famine, God sent His prophet not to any of them but to a Gentile widow of Zarephath, outside the covenant land. The point pierced their presumption: covenant privilege (being Israelites, being Jesus's townspeople) is no claim on God's grace, which is sovereign and may reach beyond the expected borders to the undeserving outsider while passing by the privileged-but-unbelieving. The Nazarenes were so enraged that they tried to throw Him off a cliff (Luke 4:28-29). To soften this point — to make Zarephath a comforting tale rather than a rebuke to presumption and a foreshadowing of grace to the Gentiles — is to lose the sharp edge the Lord Himself gave it.

Zarephath has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the reward of the widow's faith and the sovereignty of grace. The widow gave her last meal to the prophet on the strength of God's promise, and the meal and oil did not fail through the whole drought — God honoring the faith that gave its last to Him first (cf. Matt 6:33). And the place "refinery" (Zarephath) is where that faith was refined and where sovereign grace reached a Gentile widow, foreshadowing the gospel that would go to all nations. The God of Zarephath is the God who provides for those who trust Him and who shows mercy on whom He will show mercy (Rom 9:15), beyond the borders of expected privilege.
